subject: Understanding Periodogram and Comparing between individuals

messages.author: 6dafb8479e9ed914
messages.subject: Understanding Periodogram and Comparing between individuals
parts:
Hi Chris,

I hope you're doing well. I have a few questions regarding my home range analysis of satellite-tagged grassland birds from two populations. The data quality and sampling frequency vary significantly between individuals, ranging from just a few days of data to coverage throughout the breeding and migration periods. I am using Argos data, and from our previous conversation, I've decided to only use level 3 and 2 points in the analysis with an error model. However, I’ve run into a couple of questions:


1.Is it reasonable to compare the breeding season home range sizes between my two populations or between individuals, considering that different individuals were assigned different models, and the data quality varies? For example, Bird A has poor data and is assigned an IID error model, while Bird B, with better data, is assigned an OU anisotropic error model. Can valid comparisons of home range sizes still be made in this case?






2. I noticed for birds like B, with better data, most of the show a period pattern. So I went into Periodogram and looked at this:

 
If I’m interpreting the graph correctly, the red dots at half a day and one day suggest that this periodic pattern is only due to the sampling interval. Is this conclusion correct? I hesitate because when I compared day vs. night points (nest graph), it seems this bird does have a smaller roosting area at night compared to their daytime movements. 

 I also mapped Argos satellite transmission time for this bird, and it does show lower values at 6 and 19 UTC (which corresponds to 2 am and 3 pm at my study site).  I don't know how the satellites are moving above us, so I just want to make sure I am interpreting this correctly, so I don't underestimate their home range due to many points at roosting. 



3. Additionally, even among individuals with higher quality data, I’m seeing variability in how well the model fits the variogram. Bird B (from question1) seems to fit well, but Bird D here (fitted with "IID anisotropic error") shows a red line way lower than the variogram. and about five other birds look similar to Bird D.  Could you help explain this variation? The error radius should be similar among individuals because I only used the best level points. So I'm confused. 😅

 Thank you very very much!!!

Best regards,
Violet Wu

messages.author: 40fd627580dd34f5
messages.subject: Re: Understanding Periodogram and Comparing between individuals
parts:
Hi Violet,

I would use all of the location classes, and not just the best ones, unless there is some relation with outliers. The poorer location classes will be assigned proportionally larger errors in the model.
  1. Yes, the bias corrections and uncertainty estimates allow for such comparisons.
  2. From the red points in the periodogram, the variogram oscillations could be largely from periodic missingness in the data. Less movement at night could be another factor, but some of that could be sample size.
  3. When the errors are substantial in the model, this often happens and I haven't been able to figure out how to solve it, but some of the variogram variance is due to location error here.
Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Understanding Periodogram and Comparing between individuals
parts:
Hi Chris,

Thank you for your response!

To provide more context regarding the location classes from Argos: the location classes are set according to the standard deviation of the estimated location error, where LC 3 is <250m, LC 2 is <500m, and LC 1 is <1500m. LC A and LC B have the lowest accuracy, and there’s no error information associated with them.

I've run a comparison for the same bird over the same period, first using only the two best location classes (LC 3 and LC 2) and then with an additional class (LC 1). As our study bird is a grassland obligate and was never observed flying over water, the addition of LC 1 appears to increase outliers visually. So far, I’ve removed only the clear "spike" outliers and when speed > 15m/s, and have conducted analyses for both scenarios. The results show that including LC 1 more than doubles the estimated home range size.

Outliers:

          

After removing outliers:

               

                                                   LC3+LC2: 172 points                                                                                                  LC3 + LC2 + LC1： 277 points

Variogram fit (Both OU anisotropic error ):

                            

Home Range Results:

                        

Plotting:
                     

Based on this, I feel that using only LC 3 and LC 2 might better represent the bird's true range and minimize overestimation. However, if we ultimately decide to include LC 1, I’d greatly appreciate any guidance on a more objective method for removing outliers to ensure accuracy in my analysis. Thank you very very much! 

Best regards,
Violet

Hi Violet,

Are your data being correctly imported with their error ellipses? The LC 1 data, should be assigned kilometer error ellipses, and then those location estimates should get pulled in before kernel placement.

Best,
Chris
